newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says progress in China WTO talks, issues remain.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says progress in China WTO talks, issues remain.

text.p: U.S. trade officials said on Thursday that progress had been made in talks with China on its bid to join the World Trade Organisation, but many details remained to be negotiated.

"We have seen some new progress during the WTO talks this week with regard to China's commitment to meaningful market reforms, particularly in the area of trading rights which are critical to addressing our market access concerns," U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said in a statement.

She released the statement after negotiators in Geneva completed nearly two weeks of intense talks on China's WTO bid. The negotiations, launched 10 years ago, have taken on a new energy in recent weeks since China agreed to drop some of its trade barriers.
A U.S. trade official said Chinese officials made commitments on some market access issues, but the details and timing of those commitments remained to be negotiated.
One commitment, the official said, was to drop a system of state-designated middlemen and allow foreign companies to trade directly with import buyers.
"This is a very fundamental commitment," the official told reporters in a telephone conference.

Beijing has also agreed to abide by WTO rules on protection of copyrights and other intellectual property as soon as it enters the global trading body with no transition period. The U.S. official said that by contrast, Hong Kong has taken a five-year transition under the more lenient rules allowed developing countries.
"That coupled with the severe crackdown that is taking place against illegal compact disc factories and other forms of intellectual property ... is a very welcomed development," the official said.
The official said a number of issues including market access issues and subsidies remained to be worked out as well as the details of the commitments already made by Beijing.
"There are a lot of details to be worked out and we are taking a very sober view of this whole process," the official said.
On subsidies, the WTO secretariat plans to send a technical team to Beijing to help the Chinese understand the issues where "the learning curve is quite steep," the official said.
A number of important agriculture issues also remain, the official, who asked not to be identified, said.

"We have a very long way to go on agriculture, it is among our very top priorities," he said. "It is very clear to me the Chinese now have a much clearer understanding, first of all as to what their WTO obligations are regarding agriculture, and second of all, just how important this issue is to us."

He said China would send a negotiating team to the United States in mid-April for intensive discussions on agriculture issues. The United States has a number of farm trade problems with China that Washington has said needed to be resolved before it would agree to China's entry into the WTO.

The official declined to say how long it would take to complete negotiations on China's WTO bid. He said he thought European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan's assessment that it could be completed by the end of the year was "optimistic."
"It is strictly up to the Chinese," the official said. "Our approach is to let the substance drive the timing and it is really up to the Chinese."
